extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, litigants, and judges evaluating §101 patent eligibility for software/machine-learning inventions (Federal Circuit context)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria for assessing patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101—especially for claims that apply machine learning or other software techniques to generate schedules or network maps. Focuses on Alice two-step analysis as applied by the Federal Circuit to ML-related claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform the two-step Alice/Mayo analysis: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas); (2) if so, consider the elements of each claim individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether they contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the patent-ineligible concept itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote formulation from Alice: first determine whether the claims are directed to an ineligible concept; if so assess the claim elements both individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether they possess an 'inventive concept' that is 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.' (Alice, 573 U.S. at 217–18; Mayo, 566 U.S. at 72). Use this two-step framework as the governing eligibility test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look to the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the claim's character 'as a whole' by looking at the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art to decide whether the claim is directed to excluded subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'focus of the claimed advance' test (Koninklijke KPN v. Gemalto, quoted in the opinion). Ask whether the asserted advance is a specific technological improvement or merely the abstract idea implemented in a new context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software/ML-specific focus test: improvement in computer capabilities vs using computers as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: For software (including machine learning) claims, determine whether the claims focus on 'the specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities' or instead on a process that 'qualifies as an abstract idea for which computers are invoked merely as a tool.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed invention is simply using conventional computer/ML techniques as a tool to perform an abstract process, it is likely directed to an abstract idea (quoting Finjan/ Kon. KPN language cited in the opinion). Evaluate whether the specification/claims describe an improvement in computer functionality itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic ML techniques and generic computing are conventional (do not confer eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that rely on applying 'any suitable machine learning technique' (e.g., neural networks, support vector machines, regressions, decision trees, gradient boosted trees, Bayesian networks) and generic computing hardware are treated as using conventional technology and do not, by themselves, make claims patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion emphasizes that the patents' repeated statement that 'any suitable machine learning technique' may be used and that 'generic computing devices' suffice supports finding the ML and computing aspects conventional. Cited language: patents describing a list of typical ML techniques and stating use of generic processors/ computing devices. See also cited precedent that generic steps of implementing calculations on a regular computer do not transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention (In re Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior Univ. and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative training and dynamic updates inherent to machine learning are not a technological improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations reciting iterative training, dynamic adjustment, or updating models in response to real-time data are, by their nature, intrinsic to machine learning and therefore do not necessarily supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recentive's own admissions that 'the way machine learning works is the inputs are defined, the model is trained, and then the algorithm is actually updated and improved over time' support treating such steps as routine/incidental. Thus, merely claiming iterative training or real-time updating (without more) is unlikely to show an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must disclose how the results are achieved; functional claiming is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that only functionally describes results (e.g., 'generate optimized schedules' or 'unearth useful patterns') without delineating how to achieve those results in a non-abstract way is insufficient for patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion cites that claims which 'do not sufficiently describe how to achieve [stated] results in a non-abstract way' and that 'functional claim language, without more, is insufficient' (citing IBM v. Zillow, Two-Way Media, Intell. Ventures, Elec. Power Group). The patent should explain a specific implementation or method by which the purported improvement is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying existing technology to a new field or database does not make it non-abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use (e.g., event scheduling, network maps) or applying known techniques to a novel database or data environment does not render the claim non-abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion reiterates established precedent: 'An abstract idea does not become nonabstract by limiting the invention to a particular field of use or technological environment.' (Intell. Ventures, Alice, Parker v. Flook, Stanford). Similarly, use of existing technology on a novel dataset is treated as an abstract implementation (SAP Am. v. InvestPic; Elec. Power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting and processing information is an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that principally collect information (even if limited to particular content categories) and process it fall within the realm of abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion notes precedent treating information collection as abstract (Electronic Power Group, Internet Pats. Corp., OIP Techs., Content Extraction, Digitech). Be wary of claims framed as 'collecting information and performing routine analysis' without a specific technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and efficiency improvements via generic computers are not enough
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that simply perform a task faster or more efficiently than humans by applying generic computers or generic ML techniques do not make the claims patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite authority that increased speed/efficiency from applying computers (without improved computer techniques) does not create eligibility (Content Extraction; DealerTrack; Customedia). Distinguish cases where specific computer techniques produced a technological improvement (e.g., McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step-two requirement: inventive concept must be 'significantly more' than abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two, the claim must include an element or combination of elements that transforms the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application—more than merely stating the abstract idea and adding 'apply it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Alice and Mayo language: the claim must include an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into something 'significantly more' (Alice, Trinity, SAP Am., Broadband iTV). Mere recitation of using ML to dynamically generate outputs is insufficient unless the claim identifies how that use produces a technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility at pleading stage and futility of amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: On a motion to dismiss, a patentee must plausibly allege facts that, if true, would show an inventive concept; dismissal is appropriate where the complaint fails to identify claim terms requiring construction or to allege facts that could alter the §101 analysis, and denial of leave to amend is appropriate if amendment would be futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion affirms dismissal where Recentive failed to propose amendments or identify factual issues that would alter the §101 analysis, and quotes district-court standards that dismissal is proper when a plaintiff fails to identify specific claim constructions or facts needing development before §101 resolution (Recentive, Trinity). When asserting eligibility at pleading stage, plead specific structural/implementation details showing inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents claiming only the application of generic ML to a new data environment are ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'do no more than claim the application of generic machine learning to new data environments, without disclosing improvements to the machine learning models to be applied,' are patent ineligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a central holding of the opinion: courts should not allow patents that simply apply conventional ML as a tool in a new domain unless the patent discloses an improvement to the ML technology or a specific technical implementation that provides a technological advance.
